title: Reverse a String
statement:
Write a JavaScript function `reverseString(str)` that reverses the characters of an input string without using the built-in `Array.prototype.reverse()` method.

Your solution should maintain linear O(N) time complexity and handle empty strings and special characters gracefully.
edge_cases: Empty string `""`, single character `"a"`, palindrome strings, strings with emojis or spaces.
approach: Use a two-pointer approach swapping characters in an array buffer, or iterate backwards from `str.length - 1` to 0 building the result string.
starter_code_python:
def reverse_string(s: str) -> str:
    return s[::-1]
hints: Hint 1: Can you loop backwards from the end of the string to index 0?
Hint 2: In JavaScript, strings are immutable, so build an array of characters or concatenate into a new string.

title: Valid Palindrome
statement:
Write a function `isPalindrome(s)` that determines if a given string is a palindrome, considering only alphanumeric characters and ignoring cases.

For example, `"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"` is a palindrome.
constraints: Time Complexity: O(N), Space Complexity: O(1) or O(N).
edge_cases: Strings with punctuation, mixed uppercase/lowercase, single character strings, string with only spaces.
approach: Clean the string using regex `/[^a-z0-9]/gi` and convert to lowercase, then compare with its reverse, or use two pointers moving toward the center.
starter_code_python:
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    import re
    cleaned = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '', s).lower()
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

test_cases.input: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

hints: Hint 1: Normalize the string first by stripping symbols and converting to lower case.
Hint 2: Compare characters from the start and end simultaneously using two pointers.

title: Character Frequency Counter
statement:
Implement `countFrequency(str)` which returns an object mapping each character in `str` to its occurrence count.

Example:
`countFrequency('firstlabs')` => `{ f: 1, i: 1, r: 1, s: 2, t: 1, l: 1, a: 1, b: 1 }`
output_format: Object with character keys and integer counts.
edge_cases: Empty string returns `{}`. Case sensitivity should be preserved.
approach: Iterate through characters using `for...of` and populate an accumulator object.
hints: Hint: Use `(map[char] || 0) + 1` to increment counts safely.

title: Remove Duplicates from Array
statement: Write a function `removeDuplicates(arr)` that returns a new array with all duplicate values removed, preserving the original order of their first appearance.
output_format: Array containing only unique elements in original order.
edge_cases: Empty array, array with all identical elements, array with mixed types.
approach: Use a `Set` via `[...new Set(arr)]` or filter with `seen` Set.
starter_code_python:
def remove_duplicates(arr: list) -> list:
    return list(dict.fromkeys(arr))
hints: Hint: JavaScript `Set` guarantees insertion order preservation.

title: Find Second-Largest Distinct Number
statement:
Write a function `findSecondLargest(nums)` that finds the second-largest distinct number in an array in a single O(N) pass without sorting.

If no second-largest distinct element exists (e.g. array length < 2 or all elements equal), return `null`.
constraints: Single O(N) pass, O(1) extra auxiliary space. Do NOT use `nums.sort()`.
edge_cases: Duplicates of the maximum number (e.g. `[10, 10, 9]`), negative numbers, arrays with fewer than 2 distinct elements.
approach: Maintain two tracking variables `first` and `second` initialized to `-Infinity`. Update `second` when a number exceeds it but is less than `first`.
hints: Hint 1: Track `first` and `second` initialized to `-Infinity`.
Hint 2: Pay attention to when a number equals `first`—do not update `second` with the duplicate.

title: Two Sum (Indices)
statement:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the indices sorted in ascending order `[i, j]`.
constraints: Time Complexity: O(N), Space Complexity: O(N).
edge_cases: Negative numbers, zero as target or elements.
approach: Use a hash map to store `target - num` as you iterate.

test_cases.description: Standard case with elements at beginning

hints: Hint: As you iterate through `nums`, calculate `complement = target - nums[i]`. Has that complement already been stored in your map?

title: Flatten Nested Array
statement:
Write a recursive or iterative function `flattenArray(arr, depth = Infinity)` that flattens an array of arbitrarily nested arrays up to the specified `depth`.

Do not use the native `Array.prototype.flat()` method.
edge_cases: Deeply nested arrays `[[[[1]]]]`, empty sub-arrays `[[], [[]]]`, depth = 1.
approach: Use `reduce` with recursion or a stack-based loop checking `Array.isArray(item)` and decrementing depth.
hints: Hint: `Array.isArray(val)` tells you whether to recurse or push directly.

title: Implement Debounce Function
statement:
Implement a `debounce(fn, delay, immediate = false)` utility function.

When invoked repeatedly, `debounce` postpones the execution of `fn` until after `delay` milliseconds have elapsed since the last time the debounced function was invoked. If `immediate` is true, trigger the function on the leading edge instead of the trailing edge.
constraints: Must preserve `this` context and pass all arguments to `fn`.
edge_cases: Rapid successive calls, cancelling existing timers.
approach: Store `timerId` in closure. Clear timer on each call and schedule `setTimeout`.
starter_code_python: # Debounce is typically client-side JavaScript for DOM/input events
hints: Hint 1: Use `clearTimeout(timerId)` to reset on every event.
Hint 2: Be sure to pass arguments with `fn.apply(this, args)` to retain context.

title: High-Earning Engineers
statement:
Write a SQL query to find the `id`, `name`, and `salary` of all employees in the Engineering department (`department_id = 1`) who earn a salary strictly greater than 70,000.

Order the results by `salary` in descending order.
edge_cases: Employees with salary exactly 70,000 (must be excluded).
approach: Use SELECT with WHERE conditions combining department_id and salary, followed by ORDER BY.
starter_code_sql:
-- Write your SQL query below
SELECT id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1 AND salary > 70000
ORDER BY salary DESC;
hints: Hint: `WHERE department_id = 1 AND salary > 70000 ORDER BY salary DESC`

title: Department Average Salary Breakdown
statement:
Write a SQL query to display each department's name, the number of employees in that department, and the average employee salary rounded to 2 decimal places.

Columns required: `department_name`, `employee_count`, `avg_salary`.
Order the results by `avg_salary` descending.
constraints: Join departments with employees; use GROUP BY on department id and name.
edge_cases: Round average to 2 decimal places using `ROUND(..., 2)`.
approach: INNER JOIN `departments d` with `employees e` on `d.id = e.department_id`, GROUP BY `d.id, d.name`, calculate `COUNT(e.id)` and `ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2)`.
starter_code_sql:
SELECT d.name AS department_name, COUNT(e.id) AS employee_count, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

test_cases.expected: Departments ordered by avg salary: Product (86500.0), Engineering (80200.0), Sales (77333.33), Human Resources (62000.0), Marketing (61500.0)

hints: Hint: GROUP BY must include both `d.id` and `d.name`.

title: Find Second-Highest Salary
statement:
Write a SQL query to find the second-highest distinct salary across all employees.

Alias the result column as `second_highest_salary`. Your query must work even if there are multiple employees tied for the highest salary.
output_format: Single column `second_highest_salary` with a single row.
constraints: Do not rely on LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 if ties exist. Use subquery.
edge_cases: Multiple employees having identical highest salaries.
hints: Hint: Filter out the maximum salary using `< (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)`.

title: Employees Above Department Average
statement:
Write a SQL query to find all employees who earn strictly more than the average salary of their own respective department.

Return columns: `name`, `salary`, `department_id` ordered by `salary DESC`.
constraints: Use correlated subquery or window function.
edge_cases: Exclude employees without an assigned department (`department_id IS NULL`).
approach: Correlated subquery: `WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id)`.
starter_code_sql:
SELECT e.name, e.salary, e.department_id
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id
)
ORDER BY e.salary DESC;
hints: Hint: Inside your subquery, match `e2.department_id = e.department_id` to correlate each employee with their department average.

title: Identify Repeat Customers with Multiple Orders
statement:
Write a SQL query to find all `customer_id` values that have placed more than 1 order in the `orders` table.

Return columns `customer_id` and `order_count`.
edge_cases: Customers with exactly 1 order must not appear.
starter_code_sql:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

test_cases.expected: Customers 201 (3 orders), 202 (2 orders), 203 (2 orders), 204 (2 orders), 205 (2 orders), 206 (2 orders)

hints: Hint: Filter grouped aggregate records using `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` instead of `WHERE`.

title: Total Revenue by Department via Three-Way Join
statement:
Write a query calculating total revenue generated by completed orders (`status = 'Completed'`) credited to each department.

Return columns: `department_name`, `total_revenue` rounded to 2 decimal places, ordered by `total_revenue DESC`.
edge_cases: Join paths: departments.id = employees.department_id and employees.id = orders.employee_id.
approach: JOIN departments to employees, employees to orders, filter status, GROUP BY department, SUM amount.
starter_code_sql:
SELECT d.name AS department_name, ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id
JOIN orders o ON e.id = o.employee_id
WHERE o.status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
hints: Hint: Check your WHERE filter for `o.status = 'Completed'`.

title: Departments Without Assigned Employees
statement:
Write a query to list all department names that currently have zero assigned employees.

Return column `name`.
constraints: Use LEFT JOIN or NOT EXISTS.
edge_cases: All departments having employees vs one empty.
approach: LEFT JOIN employees on department_id WHERE employees.id IS NULL.
starter_code_sql:
SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;

test_cases.expected: Empty result or departments with null employee id

hints: Hint: `LEFT JOIN` keeps all departments even if there is no match in `employees`.

title: Employee-Manager Organizational Hierarchy
statement:
Write a SQL query using a SELF JOIN to list each employee's name alongside their direct manager's name.

Return columns: `employee_name`, `manager_name`.
If an employee has no manager (e.g. CEO or Department Head), display `NULL` for their manager name. Order by `employee_name ASC`.
constraints: Use `LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id`.
approach: Aliasing the same table twice (`e` for employee, `m` for manager) with a LEFT JOIN.
starter_code_sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee_name, m.name AS manager_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY e.name ASC;

test_cases.expected: 14 rows with employee names and respective manager names

hints: Hint: Alias the employees table twice: `FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id`.
